I need a sales page for my meal delivery service. I'm a registered dietitian, and I run a weekly delivery of cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes in our metro area.

Facts:
- 10 meals a week cost $129, delivered every Sunday. A trial week costs $59.
- Every meal has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less, and I plan each menu myself.
- We have 88 active customers. 37 of them have been with us more than six months.
- 14 customers shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. 10 went down, 3 stayed about the same, and 1 went up. The average drop was 0.6 points.
- I don't track whether customers changed their medication during that time.
- About 1 in 5 people who try a trial week sign up for the full plan.

I want the page to say our meals will lower your A1C. Around 400 words.

Before I write this, I need you to decide one thing and answer a few questions.

## The A1C claim

**What you want to say:** "Our meals will lower your A1C." That promises a result to every reader.

**What your numbers support:** 14 of your 88 customers chose to share their results. Of those, 10 went down, 3 stayed about the same and 1 went up, and you don't know whether any of them changed medication. That shows the meals *can* go along with a lower A1C. It doesn't show that the meals caused it, or that they'll do it for whoever reads the page.

**A skeptical reader, or their doctor, would ask:**
- Did those people also start or change a medication? Your data can't answer this.
- Are the 14 who shared typical, or are they the ones whose results were good? Your data can't answer this either.
- Is 14 people enough to go on? You can answer this one honestly by saying it's a small group and that you're telling them exactly what you saw.

There's also a practical risk. "Will lower your A1C" is a health-outcome promise. Advertising rules and your own professional code as an RD expect that kind of claim to have much stronger evidence behind it than 14 self-reported results.

**What I'd suggest instead:** Report the results plainly and let the reader draw the conclusion:

> "14 customers shared their A1C with me from before they started and after three months. 10 went down, 3 held steady, 1 went up. We don't track medication changes, so I can't credit the meals alone, but every one of those meals was planned to 45 g of carbs or less."

Being this open builds trust with readers who have heard a lot of diabetes promises before. It also keeps your strongest facts up front: a dietitian plans every meal, every meal has 45 g of carbs or less, and 37 of your 88 customers have stayed more than six months.

**Which version do you want?** I'll write either one, but I think the second is both safer and more convincing.

## Questions

1. **Is the 0.6-point average drop across all 14 people, or only the 10 whose A1C went down?** This changes how I can word it.
2. **How do the trial and cancelling work?** Is the $59 trial the same 10 meals? Can people skip a week or cancel any time, and is there an order deadline before Sunday? These matter most to someone deciding whether to try it.
3. **How do you want to introduce yourself?** I'd like your name and credentials, how long you've done this, and whether you tell customers to keep working with their doctor.
4. **What's the main reason people hesitate?** For example: taste or getting bored of the food, the price compared with cooking, or dietary needs. What can you say back to it? A sample menu, how often the menu changes, or a customer quote you have permission to use would all help. For reference, $129 for 10 meals works out to $12.90 a meal.
5. **What will readers find out after they order?** For example, where you deliver, whether they can swap meals, and how you handle allergies. It's better to say these on the page.
6. **Do you want the 1-in-5 trial-to-subscription figure on the page?** My view is to leave it off. It's useful for your business, but it doesn't help a reader decide.

Go with the second version. I can't promise anyone's A1C will go down.

1. I don't know offhand whether the 0.6 is across all 14 or just the 10.
2. I'm not sure if the trial is the same 10 meals. There's no contract on the full plan, so people can skip a week or cancel any time. Orders close Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery.
3. I'm Lena Ortiz, RD, and the service is Steady Plate. I don't have a number for how long. The meals don't replace anyone's doctor's advice.
4. I don't know the main reason people hesitate. The menu repeats every 4 weeks, and people can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices each week. I don't have a customer quote or a sample menu ready.
5. We deliver within 25 miles of downtown. Swaps work as described above. I'm not sure what to say about allergies. Anyone can also have a 15-minute phone call with me before they start.
6. Leave it off.

I've written the second version. Everything in it comes from what you've told me, and I've noted below what I left out or worded carefully.

# Steady Plate

## Cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes, planned by a registered dietitian

Knowing what to eat with type 2 diabetes is one job. Cooking it every day is another. Steady Plate does both for you.

I'm Lena Ortiz, RD. I plan every menu myself, and every meal on it has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less. You don't have to count, weigh or guess. Every Sunday, 10 cooked lunches and dinners arrive at your door.

### What I've seen, and what I can't promise

I won't promise that your A1C will go down. No honest meal service can.

Here's what I can tell you. 14 customers shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. Ten went down, three stayed about the same, and one went up. That's a small group. I also don't track whether anyone changed their medication during that time, so I can't give the meals all the credit. What I do know is that every meal those customers ate from us had 45 grams of carbs or less.

We have 88 active customers. 37 of them have been with us for more than six months.

### "Won't I get tired of the same food?"

The menu runs on a four-week cycle. Each week, you can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices. That way you're eating to a plan without eating the same thing every week.

### What it costs

- **Weekly plan:** 10 meals for $129, about $12.90 a meal
- **Trial week:** $59
- **No contract:** skip a week or cancel any time
- **Order deadline:** Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery
- **Delivery area:** within 25 miles of downtown

### Talk to me before you start

Anyone can book a 15-minute phone call with me before their first order. Tell me how you eat now, what you've tried before, and anything I should know about your diet, including allergies. You'll get your answers from the dietitian who plans the meals.

Steady Plate doesn't replace your doctor's advice. Keep working with your doctor on your medication and care. We take one daily job off your list: deciding what's for lunch and dinner, and cooking it.

### Start with a trial week

Order by Thursday at noon and your first meals arrive on Sunday. If it isn't for you, there's nothing to cancel beyond that week. If it is, the full plan has no contract.

A few things to check before you publish:

- **I left out the 0.6-point average drop.** If it turns out to cover all 14 people, you can add "the average change was a drop of 0.6 points" after "one went up." If it only covers the 10 whose A1C went down, I'd leave it out, because it makes the results look better than they were.
- **The trial week doesn't say how many meals it includes.** Add the number once you know it.
- **Allergies are only mentioned as something to raise on the call.** The page doesn't say you can accommodate them. If you can, say exactly how.
- **The closing line assumes the trial doesn't renew automatically.** It says there's nothing to cancel beyond that week. If the trial rolls into the full plan, change that line.
- **The two buttons need links.** I didn't add a website, phone number or booking link because you didn't give me any.
- **It's about 400 words.**
